American law presumes money relief, and specific relief also aims primarily to compensate, not to compel; equity's adequacy test grew out of its jurisdictional compromise with the common-law courts (C&M 929). Specific performance orders the promised act; an injunction forbids conduct that breaks the contract. Restatement § 357(2) allows an injunction where the duty is one of forbearance, or where the duty is to act and specific performance would be denied only for reasons inapplicable to an injunction. Either may issue against a party threatening breach (§ 357).

It examines Article 1221, including the significance of good faith and the comparison between the cost to the debtor and the creditor’s interest. It also discusses Article 1222’s route for arranging performance by another and the coercive payment mechanism known as an astreinte.

Specific enforcement is the central French remedy: for goods it does not matter whether they are unique, and there is no duty to mitigate (supp. 117). A creditor may claim the price itself, subject to a court's power to defer payment for up to two years (the délai de grâce). The astreinte, a mounting periodic penalty supporting an order to act, is 'unequivocally punitive' (supp. 121), whereas the editors describe American specific relief as primarily compensatory (C&M 929).

Klein v. PepsiCo, Inc.: Klein demonstrates why formation, breach, and remedy require separate analysis. It also contrasts with Walgreen’s difficult-to-measure long-term injury and Morris’s individually valued horse.

Walgreen Co. v. Sara Creek Property Co.: Walgreen explains the adequacy inquiry through the practical costs of measuring loss, enforcing an order, and negotiating a release. Economic reasoning can support specific relief as well as damages.

Commonwealth v. Cosby: This assigned remedies reading reaches back to reliance and promise enforcement. It illustrates why a course-wide concept index must cross the syllabus’s unit boundaries. Its holding is itself a form of specific relief: the court required that the promise 'be enforced' rather than compensating its breach (supp. 127).

Notes after Snow Phipps (C&M 945–947): courts may order performance because the agreement clearly provides for it; damages for delay usually accompany an order; equity would not order an opera singer to perform (De Rivafinoli) or a contractor to staff a second shift (Bliss), but construction on the defendant's land tied to a conveyance is more readily ordered (Floyd v. Watson). An arbitrator may award specific performance a court would refuse; New York enforced such an award in Grayson-Robinson Stores (C&M 947).

structuralAdditions (not registered: new.reason: Restatement § 364(1): relief 'will be refused' if it would be unfair because of mistake, unfair practices, unreasonable hardship or a grossly inadequate exchange; § 362 requires terms certain enough for an order; § 366 bars disproportionate supervision; Bliss refused relief for 'the imprecision of the contract provision' (C&M 947). K-34 sent every inadequate-damages path straight to 'Fashion the specific relief'.

new.label: Does an equitable bar defeat the order?
new.detail: Even where damages are inadequate, a court will not order performance if the terms are not certain enough to frame an order (§ 362; Bliss refused relief partly for 'the imprecision of the contract provision', C&M 947). Relief will be refused as unfair if the contract was induced by mistake or unfair practices, if it would cause unreasonable hardship or loss to the party in breach or to third persons, or if the exchange is grossly inadequate or the terms otherwise unfair (§ 364(1)). Nor will a court order a performance whose enforcement or supervision burdens are disproportionate to the advantages of enforcement and the harm of denial (§ 366). Public policy (§ 365) and an unsecured, unperformed agreed exchange (§ 363) can also bar relief.

edges.label: Terms too uncertain, relief unfair, or supervision disproportionate

structuralAdditions (not registered: new.reason: Floyd v. Watson: the agreement 'includes a provision for conveyance of land, and therefore specific performance is proper'; Bliss refused to order 300 more workers onto a steel-mill site as imprecise and impracticable to enforce (C&M 946–947). K-34 had no branch for construction, so a building contract could reach only 'Personal services' and a refusal.

new.label: Can the court frame and supervise an order for the work?
new.detail: Courts have shown increased willingness to order performance of construction contracts, mostly where the construction is on the defendant's land with a conveyance to follow (Floyd v. Watson, C&M 946). Bliss refused to order a contractor to put 300 more workers on a steel-mill modernization: the provision was imprecise, and keeping a set number of workers on the site was impracticable, if not impossible, to enforce; damages remained available (C&M 947). Section 366 states the general limit.

edges.label: Order can be framed and supervised, or the work is tied to a conveyance of land
